title: How to Evoke Re-Viewing of Insects Through an Interdisciplinary Art Project
content: The public often perceives insects as irritants, invaders, or threats. This perception is shaped both by familiarity (people tend to become aware of insects through their experiences with pests) and by unfamiliarity (most people know little about the sophisticated behaviors, morphologies, and ecological significance of insects) (Baldwin et al. 2008). Meanwhile, much of entomology focuses on controlling species of insects deemed harmful to humans or ecosystems, which can reinforce the view that insects are inherently undesirable. For instance, the red imported fire ant (Solenopsis invicta), a globally invasive species, is typically perceived only through a damage-based viewpoint, and for good reason. In the United States alone, this globally invasive species causes billions of dollars in economic losses each year (Pimentel et al. 2005). However, this framing as a pest is ethically reductive and renders invisible the ants’ complex social habits, behavioral adaptability, and intelligence—traits that, in other animals, might be praised or even mythologized.
